newsitem.title: HUNGARY: INTERVIEW - World Bank urges Hungary pension reform.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - World Bank urges Hungary pension reform.

text.p: Hungary should press ahead with plans for pension reform to take advantage of ample preparatory work already done, a World Bank adviser said on Monday.
"There is more mileage in implementing it as soon as possible, because in a few years' time adjustments will have to be done anyway," Dimitri Vittas told Reuters in an interview.

Hungary's pension reform plan, which the government hopes parliament will pass by May for introduction in 1998, is for a compulsory two-tier system, with two-thirds of contributions pay-as-you-go and one-third paid into private pension funds.
The government is under pressure to implement it quickly, as the country's ageing population can no longer be supported by the existing system which produces considerable losses.
Hungary's social security deficit was over 70 billion forints ($414 million) in 1996 compared with a target of 17.8 billion, of which the pension funds deficit was some 30 billion forints.
The 1997 budget envisages a 9.6 billion forints pension funds deficit out of a total 13 billion forints combined deficit for pension and healthcare.

Vittas said that while politicians are concerned about how the reforms may be perceived at election time two years hence, the Hungarian public also needs to be convinced of the need for restructuring the pension system.
"It is not only the politicians who think two years ahead," he said. "The public also (only) thinks two years ahead".
Vittas said the World Bank is prepared to give assistance to Hungary in the form of advice and some funding.
"We are prepared to provide loans to finance a small part of the transition costs," he said.
He expects a transition period of some 25 to 30 years, with the benefits of accumulated pension fund assets showing much sooner.
"Judging by the experience of other countries, pensions funds could easily hold one fifth of total household assets within 10 years," Vittas said.
Voluntary pension funds are already active in Hungary but despite their high growth, their assets only account for 0.5 percent of GDP, he said.
At the end of 1996 Hungary had 288 pension funds with total assets of 20 billion forints, compared with some 200 funds and five billion forints of assets a year earlier, he said.
Strong pension funds would also benefit the equities market, providing long-term stability, Vittas said.
"If you have local pension funds, the market would be much less volatile," he said. "This is one of the big advantages of having pension funds".

He added that while in the long term there was a danger that pension funds could become a dominating force in a small market like the Hungarian, this threat is partially offset by the entire market's growth and ultimately can be handled by proper regulations.

"There would be a limit on their economic power because other financial institutions will also grow," Vittas said. "At this particular point, Hungary's main concern is to get the whole system started".
